Imagine an online checkout. The Order class asks Payment to take the customer’s money.

Open Payment and look at its method list: charge, refund, validateCard, sendReceipt, logAudit, notifyUser, persistTxn. Also note the fields razorpayClient and stripeClient, and the arrows from Payment out to Razorpay, Stripe, and Database.

Questions to ask yourself: Do all of those methods feel like one job, or several? If the product team wanted Apple Pay next quarter, which classes would you have to touch? What would change if the receipt email template changed?

Inspect the diagram, mark what feels wrong (with a category and a short why), then repair.
payload.requirement: There are exactly 2 design problems to find. Inspect the diagram, mark each issue with a category and a short “why,” then repair so the design is easier to change later without rewriting Payment for every new concern or payment vendor.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: Payment owns charging, validation, receipts, audit logging, notifications, and persistence — classic god object / SRP violation. Split into PaymentService, Notifier, AuditLogger, and a repository.
hints: Count the methods on Payment. Do they all sound like “taking a payment,” or do some sound like emailing, logging, and saving?
Ask: “If the email template changes, should the payment class change?” If yes, responsibilities are mixed.
Payment is a God Object / SRP violation — pull out notification, audit, and database work into their own pieces.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: Payment depends directly on Razorpay and Stripe. Introduce a PaymentGateway abstraction and inject implementations so providers are swappable without editing Payment.
hints: Click Payment, then follow the arrows to Razorpay and Stripe.
Razorpay and Stripe are specific companies’ APIs — not a general “payment provider” idea.
DIP / tight coupling — Payment should depend on something like PaymentGateway, and Razorpay/Stripe should implement that.

title: Ride Fare Calculator Review
description: A ride-hailing app where PricingService figures out how much a trip costs based on the ride’s type and distance.

payload.briefing:
This is a ride-hailing app. When someone books a ride, PricingService figures out how much they pay.

Ride exposes a type string (economy, premium, XL, and so on). PricingService.calculate takes that Ride plus distance. Imagine the body of calculate today: branches that say “if economy do X, else if premium do Y, else if XL do Z.”

Product is already talking about bike, auto, and luxury rides. Ask yourself: which class would you open to support those? What happens to PricingService every time a new type ships?

Inspect PricingService, mark what feels fragile, explain why in plain words, then repair.
payload.requirement: Find the main design problem on this diagram. Mark it with a category and a short “why,” then repair so new ride types can be priced without repeatedly rewriting PricingService.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: PricingService must be edited for every new ride type — OCP violation. Use a PricingStrategy (or polymorphic RideType) so new types plug in without changing the calculator.
hints: Pretend product asks for a “bike” ride tomorrow. Which class do you open?
If the code is full of if (type === …) inside calculate(), that is the smell.
OCP Violation — replace the if/else chain with a Strategy (or similar) so new types plug in.

title: Login Path Under Review
description: AppController hands login to AuthService, which sits next to a UserRepository. Walk the login path and study what AuthService owns.

payload.briefing:
Login looks simple from the outside: AppController calls AuthService.login().

Open AuthService and read the method list: login, signup, issueJwt, verifyJwt, oauthGoogle, oauthGithub, startMfa, verifyMfa, createSession, sendWelcomeEmail, hashPassword. UserRepository only finds and saves users.

Try grouping those AuthService methods by topic — passwords, tokens, OAuth providers, MFA, sessions, email. Ask: if welcome-email copy changed, or JWT expiry changed, or a new OAuth provider shipped, which class would move?

Inspect AuthService, mark what feels off, explain why in plain words, then repair.
payload.requirement: Inspect AuthService, mark the issue you find with a category and a short “why,” then repair so login still works without one class owning every auth-adjacent concern.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: AuthService mixes credential auth, token issuance, OAuth providers, MFA, sessions, and email — a god object. Split into TokenService, OAuthProviders, MfaService, SessionStore, and a thin AuthFacade.
hints: List AuthService methods and put each under a heading: tokens, OAuth, MFA, email, sessions.
Would a change to welcome-email text force a deploy of “auth core”? That is a smell.
God Object / SRP — extract token, OAuth, MFA, and session helpers out of AuthService.

title: Three Services at Checkout
description: OrderService, InventoryService, and PricingEngine cooperate when a customer places an order. Trace how they call each other.

payload.briefing:
At checkout, three services work together to place an order.

OrderService can ask InventoryService to reserve stock. InventoryService can ask PricingEngine for a scarcity-related price adjustment. PricingEngine has a method that touches OrderService again (reprice).

Start at OrderService and follow every outgoing arrow. Do you ever land back where you started? What would that mean for testing one service in isolation?

Trace the diagram, mark what feels wrong, explain it in plain words, then repair the call structure.
payload.requirement: Inspect how OrderService, InventoryService, and PricingEngine connect. Mark the issue with a category and a short “why,” then repair so checkout still works and the dependency arrows no longer form a closed loop.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: OrderService → InventoryService → PricingEngine → OrderService forms a cycle. Break it with a CheckoutOrchestrator or domain events so Pricing does not call OrderService.
hints: Start at OrderService and follow every outgoing arrow until you cannot go further — or until you are back.
Pricing should be able to quote money without calling OrderService.
Circular Dependency — introduce an orchestrator (or events) so the loop disappears.

title: Order Confirmation Alerts
description: After checkout, OrderService asks Notifier to reach the customer. Notifier currently wires to EmailService and SmsService.

payload.briefing:
After an order is confirmed, OrderService asks Notifier to tell the user.

Follow Notifier’s outgoing arrows: they land on EmailService and SmsService. Those are specific delivery tools with sendEmail and sendSms.

Product is already asking about push notifications and Slack alerts. Which class would you open to add those? Does Notifier need to know the difference between email and SMS, or only that a message should go out somehow?

Inspect Notifier and its arrows, mark what feels wrong, explain why, then repair.
payload.requirement: Inspect Notifier and its outgoing arrows. Mark the issue with a category and a short “why,” then repair so a new alert channel can be added without rewriting Notifier each time.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: Notifier should depend on a NotificationChannel abstraction, not EmailService/SmsService. Inject channel implementations so new channels do not modify Notifier.
hints: Which classes does Notifier point to? Are they general ideas or specific tools?
Email and SMS both “deliver a message” — that shared idea is missing as a type.
DIP Violation — add NotificationChannel; Email and SMS become implementations.

title: Shopping Cart Checkout Walkthrough
description: CheckoutPage submits to CartService, which also talks to StripeClient and Inventory during checkout.

payload.briefing:
The checkout page submits to CartService. A cart usually knows which items are in the basket.

Look at CartService’s methods: addItem, checkout, chargeStripe, decrementStock, sendInvoice — plus a stripeKey field. Arrows go from CartService to StripeClient and Inventory.

Ask yourself: how many different “topics” live on CartService? If you swapped payment providers or changed warehouse rules, which class would move? Does a shopping cart need to know Stripe’s API?

Inspect the diagram, mark what feels wrong (you may find more than one issue), explain each in plain words, then repair.
payload.requirement: Inspect CartService and its dependencies. Mark each issue you find with a category and a short “why,” then repair so cart/checkout can still take payment and manage stock without CartService knowing a specific payment vendor.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: CartService mixes cart state, payment, inventory, and invoicing. Keep Cart focused on line items; orchestrate checkout via a CheckoutService that uses Payment and Inventory ports.
hints: checkout(), chargeStripe(), decrementStock(), and sendInvoice() — how many different “topics” is that?
A shopping cart should not need to know Stripe API details.
SRP Violation — keep cart lines in Cart; move payment/inventory orchestration out.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: CartService → StripeClient is tight coupling / DIP violation. Depend on a PaymentGateway so providers can swap without editing the cart/checkout path.
hints: Who moves money for CartService today?
StripeClient is a vendor SDK, not your business language.
Tight Coupling / DIP — put PaymentGateway between checkout and Stripe.

title: Fleet Hierarchy Check
description: FleetManager registers vehicles. Study how Car and Vehicle relate on this diagram before you change anything.

payload.briefing:
FleetManager registers things typed as Vehicle. Car has methods like openTrunk and honk, plus doors and fuelType. Vehicle has start, stop, getSpeed, and maxSpeed.

There is an inheritance arrow between Vehicle and Car. In UML, the arrow points from the specialized type toward the more general type.

Ask in plain English: which word is broader — “vehicle” or “car”? Would a bike reasonably inherit openTrunk()? Does the arrow on this diagram match how you would explain the relationship to a teammate?

Inspect the hierarchy, mark what feels wrong, explain why, then repair.
payload.requirement: There is exactly 1 issue to find. Inspect the inheritance relationship between Vehicle and Car, mark it with a category and a short “why,” then repair so the hierarchy matches everyday “is-a” language.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: Inheritance is inverted: Vehicle should be the base type and Car a specialization. Flip the hierarchy (Car extends Vehicle) or prefer composition if “is-a” is weak.
hints: Which word is broader in English — “vehicle” or “car”?
Would a bike reasonably inherit openTrunk() from Car?
Incorrect Inheritance — reverse it: Car extends Vehicle, not the other way around.

title: Logging Across Checkout Services
description: Order, Payment, and Shipping services all reach a shared Logger while handling checkout work. Study how they obtain it.

payload.briefing:
Logging is useful — the interesting part is how every service gets a logger.

OrderService, PaymentService, and ShippingService all have arrows to Logger. Logger exposes a static getInstance() method and keeps a private instance field.

Ask yourself: do these services receive a logger through a constructor, or reach into a shared global? How would you give PaymentService a fake logger in a unit test without touching that global? What if staging and production should write logs to different places?

Inspect how services reach Logger, mark what feels wrong, explain why, then repair.
payload.requirement: Inspect how Order, Payment, and Shipping obtain Logger. Mark the issue with a category and a short “why,” then repair so services can log without relying on a hidden global access path.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: Singleton Logger is misused as a global service locator. Prefer injecting an ILogger (or ambient context) so services declare dependencies and tests can substitute sinks.
hints: How do Order/Payment/Shipping obtain the logger — constructor or getInstance()?
Could a unit test give PaymentService a fake logger without touching a global?
Pattern Misuse — prefer constructor injection of ILogger over Singleton access.

title: Dashboard Report Exports
description: The dashboard asks ReportService to build a report and export it; ReportService also talks to BlobStore for storage.

payload.briefing:
The dashboard asks ReportService to build a report, then export it.

Open ReportService and list the methods: build, toPdf, toCsv, toXlsx, toHtml, toJson, and emailPdf. Building the numbers and structure is one concern; turning the same report into many file shapes is another; emailing a PDF is yet another.

Imagine product asks for Markdown export next sprint. Which class do you open? Does ReportService ever stop growing method names that start with “to”?

Inspect ReportService, mark what feels fragile, explain why, then repair.
payload.requirement: Inspect ReportService’s method list. Mark the issue with a category and a short “why,” then repair so new export formats can ship without repeatedly rewriting ReportService.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: ReportService must change for every format — OCP violation (also SRP with emailPdf). Introduce ReportExporter strategies (PdfExporter, CsvExporter) and keep ReportService focused on building the domain Report.
hints: List the toXxx methods. What happens when you add Markdown?
Building a report vs turning it into PDF/CSV are different reasons to change.
OCP Violation — plug exporters behind an interface instead of new methods on ReportService.

title: Hotel Booking End-to-End
description: A hotel flow where BookingService talks to RoomCatalog, StripeGateway, and GoogleCalendar while confirming a stay.

payload.briefing:
Booking a hotel room sounds like one feature from the guest’s point of view.

Open BookingService and scan its methods: searchRooms, hold, confirm, chargeCard, refund, syncCalendar, emailGuest, smsGuest, applyPromo, generateInvoice. Arrows also go from BookingService to StripeGateway and GoogleCalendar.

Try grouping those methods by topic — rooms, money, calendar, messaging, invoices. Ask: if PayPal replaced Stripe, or Outlook replaced Google Calendar, which class would you edit? How many reasons does BookingService currently have to change?

Inspect methods and arrows, mark what feels wrong (you may find more than one issue), explain each simply, then repair.
payload.requirement: Inspect BookingService and its dependencies. Mark each issue with a category and a short “why,” then repair so booking can still take payment and sync calendars without depending on specific vendor classes.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: BookingService is a god object spanning search, payment, calendar, and notifications. Keep a thin BookingOrchestrator and delegate to RoomCatalog, PaymentPort, CalendarPort, and Notifier.
hints: Group BookingService methods into topics: rooms, money, calendar, messaging.
Payment and calendar sync are not the same as “a booking exists.”
God Object — keep booking thin; move payment, calendar, and notification out.

expectedIssues.modelAnswer: BookingService depends on StripeGateway and GoogleCalendar concretes. Introduce PaymentPort and CalendarPort abstractions so vendors can be swapped without editing booking logic.
hints: Name the vendor classes BookingService points at.
Could you swap PayPal or Outlook without editing BookingService today?
DIP Violation — depend on ports, not StripeGateway / GoogleCalendar.
